structure.rationale: The 18 concepts follow the requester's own outline (issue #146), which this pass preserves verbatim rather than re-deriving: six parts moving from the core mental model (server/session/window/pane, first session) through daily fluency (pane workflow, copy mode, long-running jobs), to ownership (config, bindings, status line), to applied developer workflows (projects, SSH, reproducible workspaces — with Elixir/Phoenix and Rust worked examples per the notes), to automation (scripting, plugins, restoration), and finally advanced/team practice (debugging, sharing sessions, and a capstone personal system). Each concept page is expected to follow the same problem -> concept -> hands-on commands -> realistic workflow -> exercise -> common-mistake shape, which is why the shared stylesheet defines .callout variants for key-idea, warning, mistake, and exercise up front. The requester's appendix material (cheat sheet, annotated tmux.conf, bootstrap scripts, migration guide, glossary) is folded into existing pages rather than spawned as separate concepts, per the notes field, to keep the 18-concept structure intact.
structure.audience: Developers who already live in a terminal (shell, editor, git) but have never used tmux, or use it shallowly and want a deliberate, reproducible setup for solo and remote/pair work.

claims.text: tmux is a terminal multiplexer: a single background server process owns any number of sessions, and lightweight clients (terminal windows) attach to a session to display and control it.

A tmux session is persistent: it survives an accidental disconnection (e.g. an ssh connection timing out) or an intentional detach (prefix + d), because the programs running inside it belong to the server process, not to the client that was viewing it.
Detaching leaves the session running in the background; reattaching with `tmux attach` restores the same panes, scrollback, and running foreground jobs exactly as they were left.

tmux was written by Nicholas Marriott and first released in November 2007 under the ISC license, as a cleaner-codebase, BSD-licensed alternative to GNU Screen; it was imported into the OpenBSD base system in 2009 (OpenBSD 4.6).

tmux's session/window/pane hierarchy and its client-server split are what most sharply distinguish it from GNU Screen: tmux had native, layout-preserving vertical and horizontal splits from its first release, while Screen only gained autosaved split layouts much later (Screen 5.0); operations like switching windows are handled server-side in tmux, so every attached client sees the same state.

A terminal emulator's built-in tabs (macOS Terminal.app, GNOME Terminal, Windows Terminal, etc.) are owned by the terminal application's own process — there is no separate server, so quitting or crashing that application ends every shell inside its tabs at once, with no detach/reattach step available.

iTerm2's tmux integration mode (`tmux -CC`) attaches to a tmux session but renders its windows and panes as native iTerm2 tabs and split panes, so the session is still owned and kept alive by the tmux server while the client gets a native window-manager feel.

snippets.code:
tmux new -s work      # start a new named session
tmux attach -t work    # reattach to it later (any client, any machine with access)
# inside tmux: prefix (Ctrl-b) then d   -> detach, leaving it running
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

pitfalls: Assuming tmux only matters over SSH: the same server-owned persistence also protects local work from a crashed or accidentally-closed terminal app, an IDE restart, or a laptop reboot.

Confusing 'close the terminal window' with 'end the session': closing the surrounding terminal app just drops a client — the tmux server and its session keep running in the background and can be reattached; typing `exit` in every pane of that session, or `tmux kill-session`, is what actually ends it.
Expecting an IDE's built-in terminal panel to behave like tmux: it is tied to the editor process's lifetime, so closing or crashing the IDE takes every job in it down with no reattach option.

claims.text: tmux is installed from the OS package manager on every mainstream platform: `sudo apt install tmux` (Debian/Ubuntu), `brew install tmux` (macOS via Homebrew), `sudo dnf install tmux` (Fedora), `sudo pacman -S tmux` (Arch); `tmux -V` prints the installed version to confirm.
`tmux new -s NAME` (short for `new-session -s NAME`) creates a new session named NAME and immediately attaches the current terminal to it as a client.
If `-s` is omitted, tmux assigns the session an automatic numeric name starting at 0 (then 1, 2, ...) instead of a memorable one, which makes it harder to target later with `attach -t`.
The default prefix key is Ctrl-b: nearly every tmux command from inside a session is invoked by pressing Ctrl-b, releasing it, then pressing a single command key (e.g. Ctrl-b then d).
Detaching (prefix d, or running `tmux detach-client`) disconnects the client from the session without ending any process inside it; the session keeps running on the server.

`tmux ls` (short for `list-sessions`) lists every session on the server with its window count, creation time, and marks the currently-attached session; `tmux attach -t NAME` (or `tmux a -t NAME`) reattaches to a specific one by name, while `tmux attach` with no `-t` attaches to the most recently used session, not a chosen one.

`tmux new -A -s NAME` is idempotent: it attaches to the session NAME if it already exists, or creates it if it doesn't, which makes it safe to bind as a single 'go to my session' command run from any shell startup or launcher. The -A flag was added in tmux 1.8 (2013).
`tmux kill-session -t NAME` ends a session outright (kills every process inside it), which is different from detaching (prefix d), which merely stops watching it.

tmux tracks whether the current shell is already inside a session via the $TMUX environment variable it sets on attach; running `tmux` again from inside an existing session tries to nest and fails with 'sessions should be nested with care, unset $TMUX to force' rather than silently creating a confusing session-inside-a-session.

The default status line sits at the bottom of the terminal: the left side shows the current session name in brackets, the middle lists the session's windows by index with the active one marked, and the right side shows the host name and clock — all customizable later, but present unmodified from the first session onward.

brew install tmux            # macOS (Homebrew)
sudo dnf install tmux        # Fedora
sudo pacman -S tmux          # Arch
tmux -V                       # -> tmux 3.x

tmux new -s work        # create + attach a session named "work"
# ...work happens...
# Ctrl-b, release, then d   -> detach, session keeps running

tmux ls                  # -> work: 1 windows (created ...) (attached)
tmux attach -t work      # or: tmux a -t work

tmux kill-session -t work   # ends it outright, unlike detaching
snippets.note: the full first-session loop: create, detach, list, reattach, end

snippets.code: tmux new -A -s work   # attaches to "work" if it exists, creates it if not
snippets.note: idempotent create-or-attach, safe to run repeatedly

pitfalls: Skipping -s and getting a numeric session name (0, 1, 2, ...): it works, but weeks later `tmux ls` is the only way to remember what's what — name every session on purpose.

Running `tmux` again from inside an already-attached session tries to nest and fails with 'sessions should be nested with care, unset $TMUX to force'; detach first (prefix d) and reattach, rather than fighting the warning.
Assuming `tmux attach` with no `-t` will ask which session to open: it silently attaches to the most-recently-used one, which is the wrong session as soon as more than one exists.

Reading the status line's session name in brackets as a window title, or the window list in the middle as a list of sessions — the three zones (session / windows / host+clock) are easy to conflate on a first look.

claims.text: tmux's object model is a strict hierarchy: one server process holds any number of sessions; each session holds one or more windows; each window holds one or more panes, which are the actual shells/programs running side by side inside a window.

A window is a single full-screen layout (of one or more panes) shown at one time; a session is really just a named list of windows plus which one is currently active, and a client only ever displays one window of one session at a time.

Objects are addressed with a target string of the form session:window.pane (e.g. work:1.2 = pane 2 of window 1 in session work); if a target is left partially or fully unqualified, tmux fills in the current session/window/pane, which is convenient interactively but should be written fully qualified in scripts.

By default, window and pane indexes are zero-based (the first window is 0, the first pane in it is 0); this is a common surprise for people used to 1-based counting, and is controlled by the base-index and pane-base-index session options (set later, in configuration).

prefix c runs new-window, creating a new window in the current session and switching to it; prefix , runs command-prompt to rename the current window; prefix & runs kill-window (with a confirmation prompt) to close the current window and everything in it.

Window navigation: prefix n / prefix p move to the next/previous window; prefix 0-9 jumps directly to that window index; prefix w opens an interactive, searchable list of all windows to choose from; prefix l jumps back to the last (previously) selected window, a fast toggle between two windows.

prefix % runs split-window -h, splitting the current pane into a left and right pair (a vertical dividing line); prefix " runs split-window -v, splitting it into a top and bottom pair (a horizontal dividing line) — the -h/-v flags name the split line's orientation, not the resulting pane arrangement, which is the single most common point of confusion for new users.

Pane navigation and management: prefix + arrow key moves focus to the pane in that direction; prefix o cycles focus to the next pane; prefix q briefly overlays each pane with its number, and pressing that number jumps straight to it; prefix x runs kill-pane (with confirmation) to close just that pane, leaving the rest of the window intact; prefix z runs resize-pane -Z to toggle zooming the current pane to fill the whole window (and back).
Closing the last pane in a window closes the window; closing the last window in a session ends the session (and, if it was the last session on the server, the server itself exits).

prefix ! runs break-pane, promoting the current pane out into its own new window; prefix { and prefix } run swap-pane -U / swap-pane -D to swap the current pane's position with the previous/next pane in the window's layout order, without changing focus.

A pane's program exiting (e.g. the shell inside it exits) closes that pane automatically; tmux does not ask for confirmation in that case the way it does for prefix x, since the process simply ended on its own.

snippets.code:
# from the command line (outside tmux), fully-qualified targets:
tmux new-window -t work -n build       # add a window named "build" to session work
tmux select-window -t work:2           # jump to window index 2 in session work
tmux split-window -h -t work:1         # split window 1's active pane left/right
tmux select-pane -t work:1.2           # focus pane 2 of window 1
tmux kill-window -t work:2             # close window 2 and everything in it
tmux list-windows -t work              # show every window in session work
tmux list-panes -t work:1              # show every pane in window 1
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

pitfalls: Assuming % gives a horizontal (stacked) split and " gives a vertical (side-by-side) one — it's the reverse: the flag names the dividing line's orientation, not the pane layout, and this trips up almost everyone at first.
Typing 1, 2, 3... expecting to jump to the "first" window with prefix 1 and landing on the second one instead, because window/pane indexes are zero-based by default.

Confusing a new window (prefix c — a whole new full-screen layout, still the same session) with a new pane (prefix % or " — a split inside the current window) — reaching for the wrong one wastes screen space or fragments work that should have stayed in one place.
Running prefix x or prefix & out of habit and blowing past the confirmation prompt without reading it, killing a pane/window with unsaved work in it.

claims.text: resize-pane (bound by default to prefix + an arrow key held with a modifier) changes a pane's dimensions without changing the layout's shape otherwise: prefix then Ctrl-Up/Down/Left/Right grows or shrinks the current pane by one cell in that direction, and prefix then Meta(Alt)-Up/Down/Left/Right does the same in five-cell steps for a bigger adjustment.

The Ctrl-arrow and Meta-arrow resize bindings are repeatable: after pressing prefix once, tmux keeps accepting the same key (held or pressed again) for the repeat-time window (500ms by default) without requiring the prefix again, so holding Ctrl and tapping an arrow several times resizes in one fluid motion instead of one prefix per cell.

resize-pane also accepts an explicit target and amount from the command line or command prompt, e.g. `resize-pane -t work:1.2 -R 10` grows pane 2 of window 1 ten cells to the right, and `resize-pane -Z` toggles zooming the current pane to fill the whole window (the same operation bound to prefix z).

tmux ships five built-in pane layouts, cycled through with select-layout: even-horizontal (panes spread evenly left-to-right, side by side), even-vertical (panes spread evenly top-to-bottom, stacked), main-horizontal (one large pane across the top, the rest in a row underneath), main-vertical (one large pane on the left, the rest stacked in a column on the right), and tiled (panes arranged in as even a grid as the pane count allows).

prefix Space runs next-layout, cycling through the five built-in layouts in order and reflowing every pane in the current window to fit the chosen layout, which is faster than hand-resizing a layout you've fought into a wrong shape.

Each built-in layout can also be selected directly, either from the command prompt (`:select-layout tiled`) or via the default bindings prefix Alt-1 through prefix Alt-5, mapped in order to even-horizontal, even-vertical, main-horizontal, main-vertical, and tiled.

prefix Ctrl-o runs rotate-window, which rotates the panes of the current window forward through the positions of the active layout (each pane's content moves to the next slot) without changing which layout is in effect or which pane has focus's relative position.

The synchronize-panes window option, toggled with `setw synchronize-panes on` (and off again the same way), makes every keystroke typed into the active pane get sent to every other pane in that window simultaneously -- not just visible characters but backspaces and cursor movement too -- so one typed command runs identically across all of them at once.

join-pane (and its mirror move-pane) relocates an existing pane from one window into another, taking `-s` (source pane) and `-t` (target window or pane) plus an optional `-h`/`-v` to say whether it joins as a horizontal or vertical split; this differs from break-pane (already covered), which does the opposite -- pulling a pane out into a brand-new window.

Setting `set -g mouse on` in tmux.conf (or running `:set -g mouse on` for the current session) turns on mouse support: clicking a pane focuses it, clicking a window's name in the status line switches to it, dragging a pane border resizes the panes on either side of it, and the scroll wheel scrolls a pane's history -- all without leaving the keyboard-driven bindings intact.

prefix Ctrl-arrow    resize-pane, 1 cell   (repeatable within repeat-time)
prefix Meta-arrow     resize-pane, 5 cells  (repeatable within repeat-time)
prefix Space          next-layout           (cycle the 5 built-in layouts)
prefix Alt-1..Alt-5   select-layout directly: even-h, even-v, main-h, main-v, tiled
prefix Ctrl-o         rotate-window         (rotate pane positions forward)

# resize pane 2 of window 1 in session work, 10 cells to the right, from outside
tmux resize-pane -t work:1.2 -R 10

# jump straight to a named layout instead of hand-resizing
tmux select-layout -t work:1 tiled

# move a pane living in window 2 into window 1, as a new right-hand split
tmux join-pane -h -s work:2.1 -t work:1
snippets.note: verified against the OpenBSD/Linux tmux(1) manual pages

# run the same command on three hosts side by side
tmux new -s fleet
Ctrl-b %
Ctrl-b %
# ssh into three different hosts, one per pane, then:
Ctrl-b :setw synchronize-panes on
# type once -- it goes to all three panes at once
sudo apt update

pitfalls: Leaving synchronize-panes on after the job it was turned on for is done: the next command typed -- including something destructive like an rm or a service restart -- goes to every pane in the window at once, not just the one you're looking at. Turn it off the moment the parallel task is finished, and treat the status line (which tmux marks while it's active) as a thing to actually glance at.

Hand-resizing panes one Ctrl-arrow tap at a time when a built-in layout already matches the shape wanted: prefix Space (or a direct prefix Alt-N) reflows the whole window in one step and is almost always faster than nudging borders into place.

Confusing join-pane's -h/-v with split-window's: both use -h for a left/right (side-by-side) result and -v for a top/bottom (stacked) result, but because join-pane operates across windows it's easy to mistype the target and join into the wrong window's layout -- `list-windows` first if unsure.

Turning on `mouse on` and then fighting it when trying to select and copy multi-line text the OS way: with mouse mode active, tmux's own click-drag takes over pane selection and copy mode instead of the terminal's native text selection, which surprises people expecting their usual triple-click-to-select-a-line behavior (the fix -- holding a modifier key while dragging, e.g. Option/Shift depending on terminal -- is terminal-specific and worth knowing before it's needed).

claims.text: Output that scrolls off the top of a pane is not gone: each pane keeps a per-pane scrollback of past lines governed by the history-limit option, but the ordinary pane view only ever shows the current screen, so the terminal's own scrollbar (if any) and normal text selection can't reach that history.

history-limit defaults to 2000 lines per pane and can be raised (e.g. `set -g history-limit 50000`), but the change only takes effect for panes created after the option is set -- existing panes keep whatever limit was in force when they were created until they're closed and reopened; very large limits trade memory for scrollback depth.

prefix [ enters copy mode: the pane freezes (new output still arrives and is appended to the history, but the visible view stops following it), a cursor appears, and the scrollback plus the current screen become one navigable, searchable buffer. prefix PageUp is a shortcut that jumps straight into copy mode already scrolled up a page, for the common case of 'I just want to look up, right now'.

Copy mode has two selectable key tables, controlled by the mode-keys option: emacs (the default on a fresh install) and vi (`set -g mode-keys vi` -- and separately `set -g status-keys vi` for the command prompt, which is a different, often-forgotten option). Which table is active changes every navigation and selection keystroke inside copy mode; it does not change any binding outside copy mode.

In the default emacs key table: arrow keys and Ctrl-a/Ctrl-e move by character/line-start/line-end, Alt-b/Alt-f move by word, PageUp/PageDown move a full screen, Ctrl-Space begins a selection, Ctrl-w (or Alt-w) copies the selection and exits copy mode, and Ctrl-s/Ctrl-r search forward/backward.

In the vi key table: h/j/k/l move left/down/up/right, w/b move by word, g/G jump to the top/bottom of the history, Ctrl-b/Ctrl-f (or PageUp/PageDown) move a full screen and Ctrl-u/Ctrl-d move a half screen, Space (or v) begins a selection, Enter (or y) copies the selection and exits copy mode, and Ctrl-v toggles rectangle (block) selection instead of the default line-wrapping selection.

Searching inside copy mode is incremental and directional: / (search-forward, vi table) or Ctrl-s (emacs table) searches toward more recent output, ? (search-backward, vi) or Ctrl-r (emacs) searches toward older output; n repeats the last search in the same direction, N repeats it in the reverse direction.

A completed copy (via copy-selection-and-cancel, the default effect of Enter/y or Ctrl-w/Alt-w) is stored as tmux's own 'paste buffer', separate from the operating system clipboard; prefix ] pastes the most recent buffer into the active pane, prefix # lists every stored buffer (list-buffers), and prefix = opens an interactive picker (choose-buffer) to paste an older one instead of only the newest.

With `set -g mouse on`, the scroll wheel drives copy mode too: the default WheelUpPane binding checks whether the pane is already in a mode, already in the terminal's alternate screen, or mouse dragging is otherwise in effect, and only then enters copy mode automatically on scroll-up -- which is why scrolling over a full-screen program like vim, less, or htop (all of which use the alternate screen and manage their own scrolling) does not drop you into tmux copy mode, while scrolling over a plain shell prompt does.

tmux's own paste buffer is not the same thing as the operating system clipboard, so pasting into another application needs a bridge: either OSC 52 (`set -g set-clipboard on`, plus, for some terminals, a terminal-overrides tweak to pass the escape sequence through) which asks the terminal emulator itself to write to the OS clipboard and works even over SSH if the terminal supports it, or piping the copied text through an external command via copy-pipe-and-cancel bound to the copy key (e.g. `xclip -selection clipboard` or `xsel` on X11, `wl-copy` on Wayland, `pbcopy` on macOS), which requires that tool to be installed locally and does not work over a remote SSH hop unless that hop also has it.

# raise scrollback before creating new panes (existing panes are unaffected)
tmux set -g history-limit 50000

# switch copy mode to vi-style navigation and selection
tmux set -g mode-keys vi

pitfalls: Typing into a pane that looks unresponsive and not realizing it's frozen in copy mode: keystrokes are being read as copy-mode navigation/search commands, not sent to the shell, until q or Enter/Ctrl-w exits it.

Assuming a raised history-limit applies retroactively: it only takes effect for panes created after the option changes, so an already-open long-running pane keeps its old, smaller scrollback until it's closed and reopened.

Confusing tmux's internal paste buffer (prefix ]) with the operating system clipboard: a copy made in copy mode is instantly pasteable into another tmux pane, but reaching another application (a browser, a chat window) needs an explicit OSC 52 or copy-pipe bridge configured in tmux.conf -- it is not automatic on a stock install.

Expecting the mouse scroll wheel to work the same everywhere: over a plain shell it enters copy mode and scrolls history, but over a full-screen program like vim or less it passes straight through to that program's own scrolling instead, because tmux detects the alternate screen and defers to it.

Searching and getting no results because the search direction was backwards from what was expected: / (or Ctrl-s) searches toward more recent output and ? (or Ctrl-r) toward older output, relative to the cursor's current position, not the top or bottom of the buffer.

claims.text: tmux's client-server model (established in why-tmux) already solves 'keep this running after I disconnect' structurally: a job running in a pane belongs to the tmux server process, not to the client watching it, so detaching (or a dropped SSH connection) does not send it SIGHUP the way closing a plain terminal window does -- which means the old habit of backgrounding a command with `&` plus `nohup`/`disown` to protect it from a closed shell is solving a problem tmux has already removed.

monitor-activity is a per-window option, off by default, enabled with `setw -g monitor-activity on` (setw is short for set-window-option); once on, any output written to a window other than the one currently displayed marks that window in the status line.

monitor-silence takes an interval in seconds and is disabled by an interval of zero (the default); set to a nonzero value, a window is flagged once it has produced no new output for that many seconds -- a more useful signal than monitor-activity for 'the build finally stopped scrolling and is either done or stuck', versus 'the build printed a single line'.

Whether a flagged window's alert is shown only as a status-line highlight or also as an on-screen message is controlled separately by visual-activity / visual-silence / visual-bell (off by default, so a plain status-line mark only); which windows the flag applies to at all is controlled by activity-action / silence-action / bell-action, defaulting to 'other' -- act only on windows other than the one currently active, since flagging the window you're already looking at is meaningless.

Because monitor-activity and monitor-silence are window options rather than session- or server-wide ones, they can be turned on for a single long-running window (a build, a deploy, a watch process) and left off everywhere else with a plain `setw` run while attached to that window, rather than a `-g` (global) flag that would apply the setting to every window in the session.

remain-on-exit is off by default: the instant a pane's running program exits, tmux closes that pane immediately (and the window too, if it was the pane's last one), which can carry away a crash message or final line of output before anyone reads it. `set -g remain-on-exit on` keeps an exited pane open -- dead, showing its last screen and full scrollback, marked inactive -- until it is explicitly dealt with.

respawn-pane restarts a command inside an existing pane (typically one left dead by remain-on-exit) without recreating the pane or disturbing its position in the window's layout; `respawn-pane -k` forces the restart even on a pane that is not dead, killing whatever is currently running in it first. respawn-window is the same operation for every pane of a whole window.

pipe-pane connects a pane's output, from that moment forward, to an external command -- e.g. `pipe-pane -o 'cat >> ~/logs/build.log'` starts appending everything the pane subsequently prints to a file. The `-o` flag makes it a toggle: running the identical pipe-pane command again turns the pipe off. It captures only output produced after it is started, not anything already on screen or already scrolled into history.

capture-pane takes a snapshot of what a pane already holds instead of watching forward: `capture-pane -p -S - -E -` prints the pane's full retained history (bounded by history-limit) plus its current screen to stdout, where -S - means 'start at the oldest history line' and -E - means 'end at the current line'. Run without -p, the captured text goes into a tmux paste buffer instead, which save-buffer can then write out to a file.

automatic-rename (a window option, on by default in modern tmux) keeps a window's name synced to what's running in its active pane, formatted by automatic-rename-format -- but naming a window manually, whether with rename-window / prefix , or a terminal escape sequence at creation, permanently switches automatic-rename off for that one window until it is explicitly turned back on, so a deliberately-named 'deploy' window keeps that name even after the deploy command finishes and the shell prompt returns.

set-titles (off by default) additionally pushes a pane's title, formatted by set-titles-string, out to the surrounding terminal emulator's own window/tab title -- relevant for anyone reading a terminal's native tabs rather than tmux's own status line, such as iTerm2's tmux -CC integration mode already covered in why-tmux.

claims.text: tmux reads its configuration file once, top to bottom, as a plain list of the same commands available at the tmux command prompt (prefix :) or as `tmux <command>` from the shell -- there is nothing special about config-file syntax beyond one command per line.

Config file lookup order: an explicit `-f <path>` on the tmux command line overrides everything; otherwise tmux reads `~/.tmux.conf` if it exists; failing that (and as of tmux 3.2) it falls back to `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/tmux/tmux.conf`, or `~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf` if XDG_CONFIG_HOME is unset. A system-wide `/etc/tmux.conf`, if present, is read first, before the user's own file, so user settings placed after it can override system defaults.

A config file is only read automatically when a new tmux server starts. Editing it does not affect an already-running server or session until it is explicitly re-read with the `source-file` command, e.g. `tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf`; most session/window/key-binding options apply immediately on reload, though a small number of once-only startup values do not.

A common convention is to bind the reload inside the config itself, e.g. `bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display-message "reloaded"`, so re-reading the file after an edit is prefix r instead of retyping the full command.

Options live in a few separate namespaces: server options (rare -- one setting, e.g. escape-time, that applies to the whole tmux process and every client attached to it, changed with `set-option -s`), session options (changed with `set-option`/`set`), and window options (changed with `set-window-option`/`setw`). Pane options exist too but are used far less often.

Within session or window options, an optional `-g` flag controls breadth, independently of which command (set vs setw) controls which kind of object: `-g` sets the global default that every session (or window) inherits unless it has its own local override; without `-g`, the command applies only to the current session (or, for setw, the window currently attached to) -- e.g. chapter 6's `setw monitor-silence 30` with no -g, scoped deliberately to just the one window running a build.

During initial parsing of a config file at server startup, there is not yet a 'current session' for a bare (non -g) session-option command to apply to -- some such commands can fail outright with an error like 'no current session'. This is why nearly every line in a starting tmux.conf uses `-g`; a bare `set`/`setw` without `-g` is meant for the live command prompt, run while already attached to the one session or window you want to change, not for the config file.

mouse (a session option) is off by default. `set -g mouse on` is the single modern option (tmux 2.1+) that replaces the older, separately-configured mouse-select-pane / mouse-resize-pane / mode-mouse options; once on it enables clicking a pane to focus it, dragging a pane border to resize it, clicking a window's name in the status line to switch to it, dragging inside a pane to select text into copy mode, and wheel-scrolling to enter copy mode automatically.

Once mouse is on, the terminal emulator's own native click-and-drag text selection is superseded by tmux's -- reaching it again needs a modifier key held while dragging (terminal-specific, e.g. Option-drag or Shift-drag), which is expected behavior, not a malfunction.

history-limit (a window option, fixed per-pane at the moment the pane is created) defaults to 2000 lines of scrollback. Raising it, e.g. `set -g history-limit 50000`, only takes effect for panes created after the change -- an already-open pane keeps whatever limit was active when it was born, until it is closed and a new one takes its place.

base-index (a session option) sets the index of the first window created in a session; pane-base-index (a window option) sets the index of the first pane created in a window. Both default to 0. Setting `set -g base-index 1` together with `setw -g pane-base-index 1` renumbers the first window/pane to 1, lining it up with the `1` key used by the default `0`-`9` select-window bindings (chapter 3) instead of leaving the first window sitting on the `0` key at the far end of the number row. The change only applies to windows/panes created after it takes effect, same as history-limit.

renumber-windows (a session option) is off by default: closing a window in the middle of a session leaves a gap in the numbering (0, 1, 3 after closing window 2) rather than shifting the rest down. Turning it on with `set -g renumber-windows on` keeps window numbers contiguous automatically after every close.

escape-time (a server option) defaults to 500 milliseconds -- the time tmux waits after receiving an Escape byte to see whether more bytes immediately follow it (arrow keys and many other special keys begin with the same escape sequence over a terminal connection). That wait is also the noticeable pause felt leaving insert mode in Vim/Neovim inside a tmux pane. Lowering it, e.g. `set -s escape-time 10`, removes the perceptible delay while staying high enough to still recognize genuine escape sequences reliably.

focus-events (a session option) is off by default. Turned on with `set -g focus-events on`, tmux forwards terminal focus-in/focus-out events through to the program running in the active pane; Vim/Neovim use this to support `:set autoread` reloading a file the moment focus returns to that pane after it changed on disk elsewhere (e.g. a git checkout in another pane).

status (session option, on by default) toggles the status line entirely. status-position (session option) defaults to bottom and can be set to top. status-interval (session option) controls, in seconds, how often polled status-line segments (like the clock) refresh, defaulting to 15. Full status-line content and styling (status-left/status-right, colors, segments) is a separate, deeper topic than these baseline toggles.

The community tmux-sensible plugin codifies a commonly-agreed baseline of exactly this kind -- notably a near-zero escape-time and a much higher history-limit than the tmux default -- as a starting point rather than a rulebook; its own README frames itself as settings that should be acceptable to everyone, not a replacement for understanding what each option does.

claims.text: The default tmux prefix key is C-b (Ctrl-b); every prefix-table binding is invoked by pressing C-b followed by the bound key.
bind-key syntax is `bind-key [-nr] [-T key-table] key command [arguments]`; `-n` is a shorthand alias for `-T root` (bind with no prefix required), and `-r` marks the binding as repeatable.
unbind-key syntax is `unbind-key [-an] [-T key-table] key`; `-a` removes all key bindings in the given table instead of just one, and `-n`/`-T` behave the same as in bind-key.

tmux organizes bindings into named key tables; the built-in tables are `prefix` (the default table entered after pressing the prefix key), `root` (keys bound with -n, active without any prefix), `copy-mode` (emacs-style copy-mode keys), and `copy-mode-vi` (vi-style copy-mode keys), plus any custom tables a user defines.
The `repeat-time` session option controls how long (in milliseconds) a client stays in repeat mode for -r-flagged bindings before requiring the prefix again; its default is 500ms.

tmux 3.1a added the `-N` flag to bind-key so a binding can carry a human-readable note/description, and the built-in default bindings were updated to use it; `list-keys -N` (or `list-keys -1N`) shows those notes.

send-keys syntax is `send-keys [-lMRX] [-N repeat-count] [-t target-pane] key ...`; it injects literal keystrokes or named keys into a pane, which is the mechanism scripts use to drive tmux sessions non-interactively.
list-keys syntax is `list-keys [-T key-table]`; without -T it lists bindings from every table, and with -T it restricts output to one table (e.g. `list-keys -T prefix`).

`switch-client -T key-table` sets the key table the client will use to interpret its very next keypress; after that one key is consumed, the client automatically reverts to its normal table (root), which is how tmux implements multi-key custom sequences and alternate prefixes.

Pressing `prefix :` runs the built-in `command-prompt` binding, opening a one-line command line at the bottom of the screen where any tmux command can be typed without prefixing it with the `tmux` binary name.

Remapping the prefix is done with three lines: `unbind C-b`, `set -g prefix C-a`, and `bind-key C-a send-prefix` — the last line is required so that pressing the new prefix key twice sends a literal C-a keystroke through to the program running in the pane (e.g. bash/readline or a nested tmux).

Custom sequential key tables are built by chaining switch-client calls, e.g. binding a key in the root table to `switch-client -T my-table`, then binding further keys inside `my-table` — after the sequence resolves (or times out) the client falls back to the root table.

`split-window` and `new-window` accept `-c start-directory`, and the format variable `#{pane_current_path}` expands to the current pane's working directory, so `bind '"' split-window -v -c "#{pane_current_path}"` opens new splits already in the directory you were just in instead of your shell's original startup directory.

Using `-n` (root-table) bindings for common letters or arrow keys shadows those keys for every program running inside tmux, including shells and editors that expect to receive them directly.

Nesting tmux sessions means the outer tmux swallows the prefix keystroke before the inner one ever sees it; the usual fix is a distinct prefix for the inner session or a dedicated pass-through binding.

claims.text: The status line is built from `status-left` and `status-right`, whose maximum rendered widths are controlled by `status-left-length` (default 10) and `status-right-length` (default 40); content longer than the limit is truncated.
The default `status-left` value is `"[#S] "`, which just prints the current session name in brackets.

tmux format strings use `#{variable}` syntax for substitution; common variables include `#S`/`session_name`, `#I`/`window_index`, `#W`/`window_name`, `#P`/`pane_index`, `pane_current_path`, and `pane_current_command`.

Format strings support conditionals with the syntax `#{?condition,true-text,false-text}`, plus comparison operators like `#{==:#{var},value}`, letting a single status-line expression change its rendering based on session/pane/window state.

`#{?client_prefix,...}` is a commonly used conditional that is true only while the prefix key is currently active (pressed, awaiting the next key), letting a status line visibly flash a prefix indicator.

`window-status-format` (default `"#I:#W#F"`) controls how each non-current window is rendered in the status line, while `window-status-current-format` controls how the active window is rendered; both can be styled differently to visually highlight the current window.

Inline style changes inside a format string use `#[attribute=value,...]` blocks, e.g. `#[fg=colour,bg=colour,bold]`, and every subsequent `#[...]` block resets and reapplies styling from that point in the string onward.

`status-style` sets the default foreground/background/attributes for the whole status line, which individual `#[...]` blocks inside status-left/status-right/window-status-format can then override locally.

`#(shell-command)` runs an arbitrary shell command and substitutes its output directly into a format string, which is the mechanism behind ad-hoc status segments like showing the current git branch; because the command runs in tmux's own environment/cwd rather than the pane's, `#{pane_current_path}` is typically piped in explicitly so it points at the right directory.

catppuccin/tmux (and similar modern theme plugins) expose pre-built status modules as tmux user options named `@catppuccin_status_<module>`; a module is enabled by referencing it in status-right/status-left as `#{E:@catppuccin_status_MODULE_NAME}`, where the `E:` prefix tells tmux to expand the option's value as a format string rather than print it literally.
tmux-powerline and powerline-style themepacks build a segmented, arrow-divided status bar and require a patched/Nerd Font in the terminal to render their separator glyphs correctly.
tmux-themepack ships multiple prebuilt theme files loaded with a single `source-file` line, and exposes its colors/segments as overridable `@`-prefixed tmux user options.

Theme plugins are normally installed and updated through TPM: add `set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tpm'` plus `set -g @plugin '<theme>/tmux'` and a trailing `run '~/.tmux/plugins/tpm/tpm'` line, then press `prefix I` inside a running tmux session to clone and source the plugin.

Treating the status line purely as decoration instead of information wastes the one piece of persistent screen real estate that's visible no matter what program is running in the active pane.

For split-window, -h produces a horizontal split (panes side by side) and -v a vertical split (panes stacked); if neither flag is given, -v is assumed.

send-keys transmits literal characters or named keys to a target pane; text sent this way is only submitted to the shell/program once you also send the Enter equivalent, C-m, as a separate argument in the same send-keys call.

Setting the window option synchronize-panes on (via setw synchronize-panes on) duplicates keystrokes typed into any one pane to every other pane in the same window — the documented use case is running the same command across multiple hosts/shells at once.

iex -S mix phx.server starts a Phoenix application the same way mix phx.server does, but boots it under Elixir's interactive shell (IEx) attached to the running app, so you can call application functions, run Ecto queries, or hit IEx.pry breakpoints while the server is live.

mix test --stale runs only test files whose referenced modules (transitively) or the test file itself changed since the last --stale run, tracked via a manifest; the first --stale invocation always runs the full suite to build that manifest.

mix_test_watch is a third-party Hex package (not built into Mix) added via {:mix_test_watch, "~> 1.0", only: [:dev, :test], runtime: false} in mix.exs; it exposes a mix test.watch task that re-runs mix test automatically whenever a watched file changes.
Command-line arguments passed to mix test.watch (e.g. a file path, or --stale) are forwarded through to the underlying mix test invocation it triggers on each change.

mix format applies Elixir's built-in code formatter using rules from .formatter.exs in the project root; mix format --check-formatted verifies formatting without rewriting files, which is the pattern used in CI/pre-commit checks.

A generated Phoenix app splits code into lib/<app> (business/domain logic) and lib/<app>_web (Controller/View, the web-facing layer); test/ mirrors lib/'s structure, and assets/ holds front-end JS/CSS source that Phoenix's esbuild integration bundles into priv/static.
cargo-watch is a standalone Cargo subcommand crate, not part of the standard Rust toolchain — it must be installed once with cargo install cargo-watch before cargo watch works.

cargo watch -x <cmd> runs cargo <cmd> once immediately, then re-runs it on every subsequent source-file change; multiple -x flags chain commands in sequence (e.g. cargo watch -x check -x test), and if no -x is given at all, cargo watch defaults to running cargo check.

cargo fmt (backed by rustfmt) and cargo doc --open are both first-party Cargo subcommands: cargo fmt reformats source files per the project's rustfmt configuration, and cargo doc --open builds the crate's rustdoc HTML output and opens it in the default browser.
cargo test compiles and runs a crate's unit tests, integration tests, and documentation tests together in one invocation.

claims.text: ssh host -t tmux new -A -s work forces pseudo-terminal allocation over SSH (-t, required because tmux needs a tty) and runs tmux's new-session (aliased new) with -A, which attaches to the session named "work" if it already exists or creates it fresh if it doesn't — so the same command is safe to re-run every time you connect.

Detaching a client (default binding prefix d, i.e. C-b d, running detach-client) and an SSH connection simply dropping have the same practical effect on the remote work: neither kills the session, because the processes inside it are children of the tmux server, a background daemon on the remote host that runs independently of any attached client.

Reattaching later uses tmux attach -t work (or the same attach-or-create form again, tmux new -A -s work) — the session and its scrollback are exactly as left, whether you detached deliberately or the link just dropped.

Inside any shell running under tmux, the environment variable TMUX is set to the absolute path of the server's communication socket, the server's PID, and the session ID, comma-separated; this is how tmux (and scripts) detect that they're already inside a session.

Starting tmux again while $TMUX is already set — running tmux locally and then also on the remote host inside that same terminal — nests two servers; tmux may print "sessions should be nested with care, unset $TMUX to force" in some code paths, and once nested, the outer session's prefix key is intercepted by the inner session before it ever reaches the outer one.

The standard fix for nested tmux is to send the prefix key itself through to the outer session by pressing the prefix twice — by default C-b C-b — relying on tmux's built-in default key binding that maps prefix+C-b to send-prefix, which literally transmits a C-b keystroke into the active pane instead of tmux intercepting it.

An alternative to double-tapping the prefix is giving the local (outer) tmux a different prefix key than the remote (inner) one's default — e.g. local C-a, remote default C-b — so a single C-a b sends a literal C-b through to the inner session.

ssh_config's ServerAliveInterval defaults to 0 (disabled) unless BatchMode is set, in which case it defaults to 300; when set to N seconds, the SSH client sends an encrypted keepalive request through the channel after N seconds of no data from the server. ServerAliveCountMax (default 3) is how many unanswered keepalives are tolerated before the client gives up and closes the connection.

For a long session behind a NAT, firewall, or load balancer with an idle-connection timeout, ServerAliveInterval should be set comfortably below that timeout (roughly half or less) — setting it equal to or above the timeout means the keepalive can arrive too late to prevent the drop.

mosh (mobile shell) uses SSH only once, for its initial authentication handshake, then hands the session off to its own UDP-based State Synchronization Protocol; because the session is tied to an encryption key rather than a fixed IP/TCP connection, mosh tolerates roaming across networks (Wi-Fi to cellular, changing IP, laptop sleep/wake) in ways a TCP-based SSH session cannot.

mosh and tmux solve different problems and compose cleanly: mosh keeps the client-server link alive and roaming across network changes, while tmux keeps the session state (running processes, scrollback, pane layout) alive across any disconnect, including the client machine disappearing entirely — a common pattern is mosh host -- tmux new -A -s work.

Mosh's server allocates a UDP port for the session and uses SSH only for the initial handshake; firewalls that permit only outbound TCP/22 will need that UDP range opened separately for mosh to work — a real deployment limitation plain SSH doesn't have.

claims.text: tmux new-session -d -s NAME creates a session in detached mode (-d) — the server starts and the session exists, but no client attaches — which is what a setup script needs so it can keep issuing more tmux commands (split-window, send-keys) against that session before a human ever attaches.

tmux has-session -t NAME exits 0 if a session by that name exists and exits 1 (printing an error to stderr) if it doesn't; a script that redirects the stderr with 2>/dev/null and branches on the exit status can decide whether to build the session from scratch or just attach to what's already running.

new-session's -A flag collapses the has-session-then-branch pattern into one call: tmux new-session -A -d -s NAME behaves like attach-session if NAME already exists (a no-op, effectively) or like an ordinary detached new-session if it doesn't.

Because -A silently no-ops on an existing session, a script that needs to run its splits and send-keys setup only on first creation still needs an explicit has-session check first — otherwise re-running the script re-splits and re-sends commands into an already-configured, already-running session.

send-keys followed by C-m is the idiomatic way to both type a command into a pane and press Enter to run it from a script; omitting the C-m argument leaves the text sitting unexecuted at the pane's prompt.

select-layout applies one of tmux's five built-in preset layouts (even-horizontal, even-vertical, main-horizontal, main-vertical, tiled) to a window in one shot — useful at the end of a setup script, after several split-window calls, to guarantee a consistent, reproducible arrangement regardless of split order.

tmuxp (Python, pip install tmuxp) and tmuxinator (Ruby gem, gem install tmuxinator) both replace a hand-rolled shell script with a declarative YAML file describing session name, windows, and panes; tmuxp load config.yaml or tmuxinator start project build the whole session and attach in one command.

tmuxp additionally offers tmuxp freeze <session-name>, which inspects an already-running, manually-built tmux session (its windows, panes, and working directories) and generates a YAML config that reproduces it — a reverse workflow from writing the YAML first.

tmuxinator's YAML supports a root key per window (or project-wide) and a pre_window key for commands to run in every pane before its main command, letting one project file drive multiple windows rooted in different subdirectories of a monorepo.

Both tmuxp and tmuxinator can load a config file living inside the project directory itself rather than a centrally registered name — tmuxp accepts a path directly (tmuxp load ./mysession.yaml or a directory containing a recognized config file).

A plain shell script wrapping tmux new-session -d -s NAME ... has no extra dependency beyond tmux itself and is trivially version-controlled alongside the project; the dedicated tools earn their keep once the layout needs to be shared across many contributors, spans many windows/panes, or benefits from data-driven YAML rather than imperative commands.

claims.text: Every tmux command available at the interactive command prompt (prefix :) is the same command tmux exposes on the command line as `tmux <command> [args]`; there is no separate scripting API, so `tmux split-window -h` from a shell script and typing `split-window -h` at prefix : do the same thing.

Target arguments use the form session:window.pane, e.g. `-t mysession:1.2` addresses pane 2 (0-indexed) of window 1 in session mysession; window is looked up by index, ID, or (partial) name within the given session.
A target-session name is matched as an exact name, a name-start prefix, or an fnmatch(3) pattern in that order; prefixing the name with '=' forces an exact match only.

send-keys [-t target-pane] key ... sends each argument to a pane; each key is looked up as a key name (e.g. C-a, NPage) and, if not recognized as a key name, is sent as a literal sequence of characters.

C- as a key-name prefix denotes Ctrl, so C-m is Ctrl-M (carriage return); sending the key name Enter (or C-m) after a command string is how send-keys submits that command as if Enter had been pressed.
send-keys -l disables key-name lookup and sends the argument as literal UTF-8 characters instead, which matters when the text to inject could itself be mistaken for a key name.

capture-pane -p prints the captured pane content to stdout instead of writing it into a paste buffer, which is what makes it usable for scripted output-checking (e.g. tmux capture-pane -p -t pane | grep ...).

capture-pane's -S and -E flags set the starting and ending line numbers to capture (0 is the top visible line, negative numbers reach into history, and '-' as -S means the start of history); without them only the currently visible screen is captured.
capture-pane -J joins wrapped lines, which is useful when pulling a long single line of program output back into a script as one string.

if-shell [-bF] shell-command command [else-command] runs shell-command via /bin/sh (after expanding it through tmux's format rules, so #{...} variables can appear in the condition) and executes command on success or else-command otherwise, making it usable for conditional logic inside tmux.conf or a key binding.

run-shell [-b] [-t target-pane] shell-command executes a shell command in the background without creating a window; if not run in the background with -b and it produces stdout output, that output is shown in copy mode in the target pane after it finishes.

wait-for channel, used without -L/-S/-U, blocks the calling client until another tmux wait-for -S channel call signals the same channel name, giving scripts a simple rendezvous/signaling primitive between a driving shell process and commands executed inside tmux.

display-message -p 'format' prints a format-expanded string to stdout rather than the client status line, so var=$(tmux display-message -p '#{pane_id}') is the standard way to pull a live tmux value into a shell variable.

Sessions and layouts can be built entirely from the command line: new-session -d -s name creates a detached session, split-window -h/-v adds panes, and select-layout applies one of the five preset layouts (even-horizontal, even-vertical, main-horizontal, main-vertical, tiled).

After adding a plugin line and reloading tmux.conf, pressing prefix + I (capital I) fetches and clones any new plugins in the list and sources them; this is TPM's install key binding.
prefix + U updates already-installed plugins to their latest tracked commit; prefix + alt-u (lowercase u) removes/uninstalls any plugin no longer present in the tmux.conf plugin list.
TPM requires tmux 1.9+, git, and bash, and clones every plugin into subdirectories of ~/.tmux/plugins/.

tmux-sensible sets a baseline of options its authors judge acceptable to every tmux user without overriding anything the user already configured, e.g. set -s escape-time 0, set -g history-limit 50000, set -g display-time 4000, and set -g status-interval 5.

tmux-resurrect saves and restores sessions, windows, panes, per-pane working directories, exact pane layouts (even when zoomed), active/alternate session and window, and — for an allow-listed set of programs — the running program itself, via prefix Ctrl-s to save and prefix Ctrl-r to restore.

tmux-continuum explicitly depends on tmux-resurrect being installed and adds two things on top of it: continuous background saving on an interval (default 15 minutes) and, if opted in, automatic restore of the last save the moment the tmux server starts.

tmux-yank copies text to the OS system clipboard: prefix-y copies the command line, y in copy mode copies a selection, and Y (shift-y) 'puts' a selection onto the command line; it works across Linux (xsel/xclip/wl-copy), macOS (reattach-to-user-namespace or native pbcopy via set-clipboard), Cygwin, and WSL.

Each TPM-managed plugin is delivered as an executable shell script (a *.tmux file, e.g. resurrect.tmux, yank.tmux, sensible.tmux) that TPM sources via run-shell — meaning declaring a plugin means running someone else's shell code with the user's own OS permissions on every tmux launch and every config reload, with no sandboxing.

Because plugin code runs unsandboxed on every start, a short list of individually-understood plugins (e.g. sensible + resurrect + continuum + yank + one theme) keeps the amount of blindly-trusted third-party code small and auditable, versus copying a stranger's large dotfiles plugin list wholesale where most entries' actual behavior is never inspected.

claims.text: tmux keeps all session/window/pane state only in the memory of the running tmux server process; a full system reboot terminates that server and loses the state entirely unless it was persisted to disk beforehand — this is the specific gap tmux-resurrect and tmux-continuum close.
tmux-resurrect saves manually with prefix Ctrl-s and restores manually with prefix Ctrl-r.

A tmux-resurrect save captures all sessions, windows, and panes and their order; each pane's current working directory; exact pane layouts within windows (even when a pane is zoomed); the active and alternate session; the active and alternate window per session; which window has focus; the active pane per window; and grouped sessions.
By default only a conservative allow-list of programs is restored as a running program rather than a bare shell: vi, vim, nvim, emacs, man, less, more, tail, top, htop, irssi, weechat, mutt.

The allow-list is extended with set -g @resurrect-processes 'proc1 proc2 ...' in tmux.conf, a space-separated list where multi-word invocations must be double-quoted, e.g. set -g @resurrect-processes 'ssh psql mysql sqlite3'.

@resurrect-processes supports a leading tilde to match any process whose full command line merely contains the given substring, an arrow -> to substitute a friendlier command name when restoring, and a trailing space-asterisk (' *') to preserve the original arguments in that substituted command.

Setting @resurrect-processes to the special value ':all:' restores every detected running program, which the plugin's own documentation calls dangerous because tmux-resurrect cannot know a command's context — e.g. a destructive one-off like sudo mkfs.vfat /dev/sdb could be re-executed against a different disk after reboot.
Setting @resurrect-processes to 'false' disables program restoration entirely, so every pane comes back as a plain shell in its saved working directory.
Pane scrollback/text content restoration is a separate opt-in feature enabled with set -g @resurrect-capture-pane-contents 'on'.

tmux-continuum lists tmux-resurrect as a required dependency and adds continuous saving of the tmux environment on a timer, defaulting to every 15 minutes, running in the background via a hook in status-right (so continuum requires the status line to be on).
The autosave interval is configurable in minutes with set -g @continuum-save-interval 'N' (e.g. '60' for hourly); setting it to '0' disables automatic saving entirely.

Automatic restore on tmux start is opt-in via set -g @continuum-restore 'on' and, per the plugin's own docs, happens exclusively when the tmux server itself starts — no other action such as sourcing tmux.conf triggers it.

tmux-resurrect is idempotent on restore: it will not recreate panes or windows that already exist, with one exception — the single pane present when tmux was started specifically to perform a restore is overwritten.
tmux-resurrect automatically prunes its own saved-environment backups, removing files older than 30 days while always keeping at least the 5 most recent copies.

What gets restored is only the command line used to relaunch a program in a pane, not that program's in-memory state — e.g. a REPL (irb, python, psql) restarts with no loaded variables or open transaction, which is why restoring vim/neovim's actual editor session (buffers, undo, etc.) is documented as a distinct, separate opt-in tmux-resurrect feature layered on top of plain process restoration.

snippets.note: Extend the default allow-list of programs that get relaunched (not just a bare shell) on restore.

snippets.note: Match any process whose command line contains 'rails server' (~), display it back as just 'rails server' (->), and keep its original arguments (trailing *).

set -g @continuum-save-interval '60'
set -g @continuum-restore 'on'

pitfalls: Toggling @continuum-restore only takes effect on the next full tmux SERVER start, not on tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf — testing it requires killing the server (e.g. tmux kill-server) and starting tmux fresh.
@resurrect-processes ':all:' is explicitly flagged as dangerous in the plugin's own docs because it can re-run a destructive one-off command against different hardware after a reboot.

A restored program only gets its command line relaunched; any state that lived in the process's memory (REPL variables, an open database transaction, an unsaved editor buffer) is not restored, even though the pane visually looks like it picked back up.

@resurrect-capture-pane-contents can misbehave if the tmux default-command option contains && or || operators — the docs flag this as a known issue, best avoided by letting tmux-sensible manage default-command.

tmux-continuum's periodic save is driven by a status-right hook and requires the status line to be on; a theme plugin that overwrites status-right after continuum loads can silently stop autosave unless continuum is placed last in the TPM plugin list.

claims.text: tmux -v requests verbose logging: log messages are saved into tmux-client-PID.log and tmux-server-PID.log files in the current directory, where PID is the PID of the server or client process.
Passing -v twice (-vv) additionally generates a tmux-out-PID.log file containing a copy of everything tmux writes to the terminal.
Sending SIGUSR2 to a running tmux server process toggles verbose logging on (as if -v were passed at startup) and off, without restarting the server.

tmux list-keys lists key bindings using the same syntax as bind-key commands, so its output is the actual current binding for every key — the way to catch a config typo or a later bind-key line that silently overrode an earlier one.

list-keys -T key-table restricts the listing to one key table (e.g. prefix or root), and -N lists only keys that carry an attached note; there is no dedicated 'info' subcommand in tmux — for internal state the documented tools are show-messages, list-sessions, list-clients, and display-message -p.

show-options -g and show-options -g -w (the legacy alias show-window-options -g, alias showw, still exists) print the actual current global session/window option values the server is running with — useful when a tmux.conf change doesn't seem to have taken effect.
Options are scoped to server, session, window, or pane. A session or window with no explicit value for an option inherits it from the corresponding global option.

Running set-option without -g while already inside a live session sets that option only for the current session (or, with -w, the current window), not the global default — so the value looks changed in that one place but every new session or window still gets the old global value.
tmux loads its configuration file(s) only once, when the server process starts; editing ~/.tmux.conf has no effect on an already-running server until tmux source-file <path> is run explicitly.
default-terminal sets the default value of the TERM environment variable for new windows in a session; for tmux to work correctly this option must be set to screen, tmux, or a derivative of either.

tmux exports a TMUX environment variable inside every pane in the form socket-path,pid,session-id; tmux itself reads this variable at startup, which is how it detects it's already running inside a session and guards against accidental nesting.
The -2 command-line flag forces tmux to assume the terminal supports 256 colors and is exactly equivalent to -T 256.

terminal-overrides lets individual terminfo(5) capabilities be overridden per matching terminal-type glob pattern; the common truecolor workaround appends a Tc capability to a 256-color terminal-type pattern, e.g. set -ga terminal-overrides ',xterm-256color:Tc'. The newer option terminal-features (tmux 3.2+) has an explicit RGB feature meaning 'supports RGB colour with SGR escape sequences,' e.g. set -as terminal-features ',xterm-256color:RGB'.

respawn-pane reactivates a pane whose command has already exited; it refuses to run on a pane whose command is still alive unless -k is given, which kills any existing command first — this is the way to recover a hung/dead pane without tearing down the whole window.
kill-server kills the tmux server and every attached client and destroys all sessions it was running, with no confirmation prompt and no undo.
The default server socket lives in a directory named tmux-UID under $TMUX_TMPDIR (or /tmp if unset); tmux creates this directory itself and it must not be world readable, writable or executable.

snippets.note: Start (or attach) with verbose logging; writes tmux-client-PID.log and tmux-server-PID.log to the current directory.

tmux

pitfalls: Setting an option without -g inside a running session only changes that one session/window, so a live test can look like your global tmux.conf edit didn't take even though it will apply correctly to brand-new sessions.
tmux.conf is read once when the server starts; editing the file never affects an already-running server until you run source-file (or kill and restart the server).
$TERM outside tmux and $TERM inside tmux are deliberately different values (controlled by default-terminal) — assuming they should match is a common misdiagnosis of color bugs.
There is no 'tmux info' command in tmux; reach for show-messages, list-sessions, list-clients, or display-message -p instead when you need internal server/terminal state.
respawn-pane refuses to touch a pane whose command is still alive unless you pass -k, so a hung-but-not-yet-exited pane needs respawn-pane -k, not a bare respawn-pane.

kill-server destroys every session with no confirmation and no undo — anything not already checkpointed is gone, which is the practical argument for session-persistence tooling like tmux-resurrect/continuum before you're ever forced to reach for kill-server.

claims.text: tmux is a client-server program: every client that attaches to the same server (same default socket, or the same path given to -S socket-path) is talking to the same session, panes, and processes in real time.

By default the per-user socket directory must not be world readable, writable, or executable, so out of the box only the same Unix user can attach; sharing with a second person requires either a shared login/account or explicitly loosened permissions on a named socket (e.g. a -S-specified socket path with chmod 777).

tmux has no read-only mode by default: a second client that attaches normally with tmux attach -t session can type into any pane exactly as the first client can, because all attached clients drive the same underlying processes.

Because any normally-attached client can type, native session sharing shares whatever privilege level the session's shell already has (including active sudo/root), and tmux keeps no built-in record of which attached client sent which keystrokes.

attach-session -r is an alias for -f read-only,ignore-size: while a client is read-only, only keys bound to detach-client or switch-client have any effect, so that client can watch the session but cannot type into or resize it — the one built-in mitigation for one-way pairing.

attach-session -d detaches any other client already attached to the target session — useful for reclaiming a session solo, but leaving -d off is what allows two clients to stay attached and share the session simultaneously.

tmate is a maintained fork of tmux built specifically for instant terminal sharing; running the bare tmate command starts a session and, with zero server configuration, prints ready-to-use connection strings — no shared OS user account, no manual socket permissions, and no inbound port to open on the host, because the host makes an outbound SSH connection to a tmate server.

tmate prints (and tmate show-messages reprints) four connection strings by default: a read-write SSH session (ssh <token>@<region>.tmate.io), a read-only SSH session (ssh ro-<token>@<region>.tmate.io), a read-write web link, and a read-only web link.

By default, a tmate session's traffic is relayed through tmate.io's own public servers, which act as a proxy between the two attached ends — a materially different trust model from native tmux sharing on a machine both people already have access to, since a third-party service now sits on the connection path.

tmate can be self-hosted by running the open-source tmate-ssh-server and pointing tmate clients at it via ~/.tmate.conf (tmate-server-host, tmate-server-port, tmate-server-rsa-fingerprint), which removes the third-party relay from the picture at the cost of running and exposing that server yourself.

tmate connection strings are randomly generated per session and are the entire onboarding step: the remote person needs only an SSH client (or a browser for the web links) — no account on your machine and no network path to it.

Native tmux session sharing on a machine or LAN you and the other person already have trusted access to avoids the extra network hop and (self-hosting aside) the third-party relay that tmate always introduces, making it the simpler choice for that situation.

tmate is the better fit when the other person is remote and unprovisioned on your machine and you need a shareable link fast — it needs no user creation, no socket chmod, and no firewall/port-forwarding change on your end, unlike setting up native multi-user socket access.

tmux -S /tmp/shared_socket new -s pair
chmod 777 /tmp/shared_socket
snippets.note: Quick ad hoc two-person share on the same machine: an explicit socket path plus loosened permissions.

snippets.code: tmux -S /tmp/shared_socket attach -t pair
snippets.note: The second (or third) person attaches to the same socket and can immediately type into the shared session.

snippets.code: tmux attach -t pair -r
snippets.note: Read-only attach: the viewer can watch but only keys bound to detach-client/switch-client work.

snippets.code: tmux attach -t pair -d
snippets.note: Detach whoever else is attached before taking over the session solo (the opposite of sharing).

snippets.code: tmate
snippets.note: No config needed: starts a session and prints ssh/web read-write and read-only connection strings.

snippets.code: tmate show-messages
snippets.note: Reprint the connection strings if the startup banner already scrolled off.

snippets.code:
# ~/.tmate.conf on the client, pointing at a self-hosted relay:
set -g tmate-server-host "relay.example.com"
set -g tmate-server-port 22
set -g tmate-server-rsa-fingerprint "SHA256:..."
snippets.note: Route tmate through your own tmate-ssh-server instead of the public tmate.io relay.

pitfalls: Attaching normally (without -r) always grants full write access — tmux enforces no per-client permission model inside one session, so sharing to watch only happens if you remember the -r flag yourself.

The person you share a native session or socket with inherits the privilege level of whatever shell they land in, including any already-active sudo, so casual native sharing on a live production box is effectively casual root-sharing.

tmate's official servers are, by design, an intermediary on the connection; if that's unacceptable for your network or compliance needs, the fix is self-hosting tmate-ssh-server, not trying to tweak encryption settings on the public service.
A tmate connection string is a bearer credential — anyone holding it can attach — so treat pasting one into a public channel the same as pasting a session password.
